title: Pumping a swing with nobody pushing
interaction: Sit on a swing and tap to stand up or crouch: stand at the bottom of each pass and crouch at the ends, and the swing goes higher and higher with no one pushing; do it at the wrong moments and it dies away. A trace shows each swing's height over time; a second rider pumps seated by leaning back and forward instead. Shorten the chains and feel the timing change.
takeaway: You pump a swing by lifting yourself at the bottom and dropping at the ends, and only the right timing adds to the swing.
pitfall: Pumping is not pushing against the air or the chains: the swing gains because you lift your weight when the chain is tight at the bottom and let it drop at the ends. The rhythm is twice per swing, not once.
why: NGSS 3-PS2-2, patterns in motion, whose examples include a child swinging on a swing, https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/3-ps2-2-motion-and-stability-forces-and-interactions
overlapWith: oscillations-resonance: that page drives a pendulum with an outside periodic push; this page has no outside push at all, the rider pumps by changing the swing's length, which is a different mechanism.
needsSource: none (variable-length pendulum; the seated pumping is a stated simplification)

title: Swings & pendulums
interaction: Two swings hang side by side; put a big child on one and a small child on the other, release them together, and they swing in step. Lengthen one swing's chains and it falls behind the other, beat by beat. Push one harder and it swings further out but keeps the same beat; a metronome and a grandfather clock sit beside them, keeping time by the same rule.
takeaway: How fast a swing swings depends on how long it is, not on who is sitting in it or how hard it was pushed.
pitfall: A heavier child does not swing slower, and a bigger push does not make the swing go faster, only further; both are common guesses the page must disprove on screen.
why: Signal not verified this session (web-search budget was exhausted); expected signals: NGSS 3-PS2-2 (patterns in motion that predict future motion, with a child on a swing as the clarification example) and PhET 'Pendulum Lab'. KS2 Year 5 'Forces' (gravity, mechanisms) is the nearest verified standard https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: oscillations-resonance: that page sets mass, stiffness and damping and plots amplitude against a driving frequency; this one has two swings, one control at a time, no plot and no driving, and exists to show that weight and push do not change the beat.
needsSource: none; the full pendulum equation (no small-angle shortcut) with light damping, run for two pendulums at once.

title: Temperature & what the hand feels
interaction: Touch things around a room (a metal spoon, a wooden spoon, a wool hat, a tiled floor) with a hand that feels how fast heat leaves it, then with a thermometer that reads its own temperature once it has settled: the thermometer says they are all the same, the hand says the metal is colder. Put the thermometer in a kettle and watch its liquid climb as its particles jiggle harder. Pour a cup of boiling water into a bath of warm water and see which temperature wins.
takeaway: Things that have sat in the same room are all at the same temperature; what the hand feels is how fast heat flows out of it, which is why metal feels colder than wood.
needs: Thermal conductivity, density and heat capacity for a handful of materials (handbook values).
pitfall: Metal in a room is not colder than wood; it only takes heat from the hand faster. And temperature is not the amount of heat: a warm bath holds far more heat than a cup of boiling water.
why: Veritasium, 'Why Does Metal Feel Colder Than Wood If They're Same Temp?' (Misconceptions About Temperature), as listed by STEM Learning UK https://stem.org.uk/rxeyxn ; KS3 physics 'Energy' (heating and thermal equilibrium: a temperature difference leads to energy transfer from the hotter to the cooler object) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page turns a temperature knob to melt and boil a box of molecules; this one is about what a thermometer and a hand each measure, and why they disagree.
needsSource: One-dimensional heat conduction between skin and object (the rate set by each material's conductivity and heat capacity), a thermometer as a small thermal mass, mixing by heat capacity. Material values from a handbook table (Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0, or a textbook).

title: Thermos flasks & keeping things warm
interaction: Pour hot tea into a bare mug, a mug with a lid, a foam cup and a vacuum flask and watch four thermometers fall over an hour at different rates, with heat shown leaking through the walls, out of the open top and as a glow from the surface. Swap the wall material, add a lid, pump the air out of the double wall and silver it, and see which change stops which leak; then fill them with iced water and watch the same walls keep the cold in.
takeaway: A drink cools by heat leaking through its walls, out of its open top and as a glow, and a flask stays hot by blocking each route in turn: a vacuum for the walls, a lid for the top and a mirror for the glow.
pitfall: A flask does not make heat or 'keep the cold in' as if cold were a substance: it slows heat flow in either direction, and metal feels cold only because it conducts heat away fast.
why: KS2 science, Year 5 Properties and changes of materials: compare everyday materials as thermal insulators (primary national curriculum, https://dera.ioe.ac.uk/18300/1/PRIMARY_national_curriculum.pdf); NGSS 4-PS3-2, energy transferred by heat (https://www.cpp.edu/respect/resources/documents_4th/gr4.et_ngss.pdf).
overlapWith: entropy: that page mixes fast and slow particles and counts microstates at level 2; here heat flows out of a cup by three named routes and the page is about slowing each one.
needsSource: none

title: Toaster
interaction: Push the lever down and watch current flow through the thin wires, which heat up and glow a colour that follows their temperature, from dull red to orange. Set the browning dial and watch the bread's surface darken, faster near the wires than far from them, until the timer releases the latch; turn the dial up and down to see that it changes the time the bread spends there, not the heat of the wires.
takeaway: The wires glow because they are hot, and their colour tells how hot; the dial only sets how long the bread sits in front of them.
needs: The wire's glow colour comes from Planck's law weighted by the CIE 2 degree colour-matching functions already shipped for vision-color (`src/routes/vision-color/cone-data.ts`, read from CVRL's copy of the CIE 2012 XYZ functions; CVRL states no licence, recorded as unconfirmed in docs/DATA-SOURCES.md). A published blackbody-to-sRGB fit would avoid the data. The browning rate is a stated simplification (faster when hotter), not measured data.
pitfall: The wire does not glow because electricity is light: it glows because it is hot, and a higher setting on most toasters makes the bread stay longer, not the wires hotter.
why: NGSS 4-PS3-2: energy can be transferred from place to place by light, heat and electric currents (https://www.cpp.edu/respect/resources/documents_4th/gr4.et_ngss.pdf); nearest standard, no toaster-specific signal was found before the search budget ran out.
overlapWith: stars: that page links a star's colour to its temperature at level 2 with spectra and a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram; here the same rule is read off a toaster wire, with no spectrum or diagram.
needsSource: CIE colour-matching functions via CVRL, already shipped for vision-color (no licence stated at source; unconfirmed in docs/DATA-SOURCES.md), or a published blackbody-colour approximation needing no data

title: How a touchscreen feels your finger
interaction: Drag a finger over a screen whose glass is made see-through: under it is a grid of thin crossing wires, and at every crossing a small store of charge that your finger, a bag of salty water, draws a little from when it comes near. The grid lights up where the draw is biggest and the phone marks the spot between the brightest crossings. Press harder and nothing changes; put on a woollen glove and the glow fades to nothing; add a second finger and a second spot appears; drip water on the glass and a false spot wanders.
takeaway: A touchscreen does not feel pressure: it notices where your body draws a little charge from a grid of crossings under the glass, which is why gloves and water confuse it and pressing harder does nothing.
needsSource: none; mutual capacitance at each crossing reduced in proportion to the overlap with a conductive footprint, then a centroid between the strongest crossings.
pitfall: No pressure and no warmth is sensed (older resistive screens did sense pressure; say so). The finger does not conduct electricity into the phone; it only needs to be near. A plastic stylus does nothing, and a touchscreen stylus works because its tip is conductive.
why: 'Touchscreen' averaged about 12,200 views a month on English Wikipedia in 2025 (https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/metrics/pageviews/per-article/en.wikipedia/all-access/user/Touchscreen/monthly/2025010100/2025123100).
overlapWith: electric-circuits (level 1) has charge flowing in wires and electromagnetism (level 2) has fields and charges; here the model is a grid of capacitances reduced under a conductive footprint and a peak-finding rule.

title: Train wheels: why trains stay on the rails
interaction: Roll a pair of train wheels joined by an axle along two rails and nudge it sideways: because each wheel is a slight cone, the side pushed outward rides on a bigger circle and runs faster, and the pair swings back to the middle, wobbling less and less. Swap in flat wheels and the pair drifts to the rail's edge and leans on its flange; make the cone steeper and the wobble gets wilder. Send the pair round a curve and watch it steer itself with no differential.
takeaway: A train steers itself because its wheels are cones: whichever side rides up onto the bigger part of the cone turns the axle back toward the middle.
pitfall: The flanges do not steer the train: on straight track they rarely touch the rail, and a train running on its flanges squeals and wears. The wheels are not free to spin separately as a car's are; they are fixed to one axle, which is why the cone is needed.
why: Feynman's explanation of conical train wheels, retold in Tadashi Tokieda's widely shared video, https://kottke.org/21/10/the-simple-physics-trick-that-helps-trains-stay-on-their-tracks
overlapWith: oscillations-resonance: that page is a mass on a spring and a pendulum; the wheelset's wobble is a geometric oscillation on rails with no spring at all, and the page is about steering, not resonance.
needsSource: none

title: Vibrations & sound
interaction: Twang a ruler held over the edge of a table: the strip wobbles, and a row of air particles passes the push along to an ear, each one jiggling in place while the squeeze travels down the row; the speakers play the note. Slide the ruler in to shorten it and the wobble quickens and the note rises; twang it harder and the wobble widens and the note gets louder. Move the ear away and the sound fades, then pump the air out of a jar around a ringing bell and nothing arrives at all.
takeaway: A sound is a wobble passed along through the air: a faster wobble is a higher note, a bigger wobble a louder one, and with no air nothing reaches the ear.
pitfall: Sound does not travel as air flying from the source to the ear; each bit of air jiggles in place and passes the push on. Louder is not higher: loudness and pitch are two different things.
why: KS2 Year 4 'Sound' (sounds are made by something vibrating; vibrations travel through a medium to the ear; sounds get fainter with distance) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study ; Bartosz Ciechanowski, 'Sound' https://ciechanow.ski/sound/
overlapWith: waves-interference: that page puts two sources in a ripple tank and finds a string's harmonics; this one has a single vibrating ruler and a single row of air particles, no interference, no harmonics, just pitch, loudness, distance and the need for air.
needsSource: none; a vibrating strip whose rate rises as it is shortened (cantilever), a one-dimensional chain of masses and springs for the air, loudness falling with distance, and synthesised tones through Web Audio.

title: Washing machine spin
interaction: Load wet clothes into a drum with holes and spin it up with a speed slider: the drum keeps pushing the clothes round in a circle, but the water at the holes gets no push and leaves in a straight line, tangent to the drum, into the outer tub, with a trail showing each drop's straight path. Spin faster to shed more water, then pile the clothes on one side and watch the drum thump and walk, and spread them out to fix it.
takeaway: Nothing throws the water outward: the drum keeps turning the clothes while the water at the holes simply carries straight on, and the faster the drum, the more water escapes.
pitfall: Do not say a centrifugal force flings the water out: seen from the room the water moves in a straight line and it is the drum that turns away from it.
why: Nearest standard: KS3 physics forces, where a force is needed to change the direction of motion (STEM Learning KS3 forces collection, https://www.stem.org.uk/node/15878). No page-specific signal was found before the search budget ran out.
overlapWith: newtons-laws: that page shows forces changing motion on a straight track; here the straight path is what the water takes when the drum stops pushing it, and the circle belongs to the drum.
needsSource: none

title: Water pressure & hydraulics
interaction: Punch holes at different heights in a tall bottle and the jets reach different distances, the lowest furthest. Lower a gauge into a lake, then into a thin tube of the same depth: it reads the same, deeper means harder, however wide or narrow the water. Push down on the small piston of a hydraulic lift and the big piston raises a car with a far bigger push, but rises a far shorter way; try the same with a bicycle brake and a digger's arm.
takeaway: Water pushes harder the deeper you go, whatever the shape of the container, and a liquid passes a push along so that a small push on a small piston becomes a big push on a big one that moves less far.
pitfall: Pressure depends on depth, not on how much water there is: a thin tube and a lake push equally hard at the same depth. And a hydraulic lift is not free work; the big piston moves as much less as it pushes more.
why: PhET 'Under Pressure' (pressure, density, fluids) https://phet.colorado.edu/en/simulations/under-pressure ; KS3 physics 'Pressure in fluids' (pressure in liquids, increasing with depth) and KS2 Year 5 'Forces' (mechanisms that allow a smaller force to have a greater effect) https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: bridges-structures: that page carries loads through beams and cables; this one carries a push through a liquid, and shows that depth, not width, sets the pressure.
needsSource: none; hydrostatic pressure growing with depth, jets from Torricelli's law, Pascal's principle with volume conservation between the two pistons.

title: Pressure in fluids & buoyancy
interaction: Drag an object of adjustable volume and density into a tank of water and watch it sink, hover or float: arrows show the pressure growing with depth on every face, and the net upward push equals the weight of the water the object displaces, drawn as a bar beside the object's own weight. Lower a diver with a pressure gauge down the column, swap the water for oil or brine, then press on the small piston of a hydraulic lift to raise a car on the large one.
takeaway: Pressure in a fluid grows with depth and pushes in every direction, so a submerged object is pushed harder from below than from above, and it floats when that difference exceeds its weight.
needsSource: none; the densities of water, brine, oil, ice, wood and steel are standard reference values
pitfall: Buoyancy is not a special force of water: it is the ordinary pressure difference between an object's bottom and its top. Floating does not need a lot of water around the object; a ship floats in a snug dock, and the upthrust depends on the fluid displaced, not on how much fluid is left.
why: AQA GCSE Physics 8463 topic 4.5.5 'Pressure and pressure differences in fluids' (pressure with depth, upthrust, atmospheric pressure) https://filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/physics/specifications/AQA-8463-SP-2016.PDF ; AP Physics 1 Unit 8 'Fluids' carries 10 to 15% of the exam https://apstudents.collegeboard.org/courses/ap-physics-1
overlapWith: states-of-matter runs a particle box with pressure as a control and flight shows lift on a wing; neither shows pressure growing with depth or the upthrust that follows from it. The pool's level-0 water-pressure-and-hydraulics and air-pressure-and-straws feel the push without the force balance.

title: Gas laws: pressure, volume & temperature
interaction: Pump molecules into a cylinder with a movable piston and a heater; the pressure is measured by counting molecules hitting the walls, not read from a formula. Hold the temperature and squeeze the piston to trace pressure against volume; hold the volume and heat the gas to trace pressure against temperature, then extend that line back to where the pressure would reach zero and find absolute zero. Pump up a bicycle tyre to see why it warms.
takeaway: Gas pressure is molecules hitting the walls, so halving the volume doubles the pressure and heating a sealed container raises it, and tracing the pressure back to zero points to a lowest possible temperature.
needsSource: none
pitfall: The three laws hold for a fixed amount of gas and absolute temperature: pressure against degrees Celsius is a straight line that misses the origin. Squeezing a gas quickly warms it, so a quick squeeze is not a constant-temperature experiment.
why: AQA GCSE Physics 8463 topic 4.3.3 'Particle model and pressure' (gas pressure and temperature, pressure and volume) https://filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/physics/specifications/AQA-8463-SP-2016.PDF ; PhET's 'Gas Properties' (pump molecules, change volume, add heat, measure pressure) is one of its most used simulations https://phet.colorado.edu/en/search?q=Thermo
overlapWith: states-of-matter runs a molecular box through freezing, melting and boiling with temperature and pressure as controls; this page stays in the gas phase and measures the three relationships between pressure, volume and temperature that the phase page never plots.

title: Magnets & electromagnets
interaction: Drag bar magnets around a board scattered with compass needles and iron filings; the field, computed from the magnets' poles, redraws as they move, and a meter shows the pull between two magnets falling as they are separated. Wind a coil around an iron core, set its current and number of turns, and lift a stack of paper clips; reverse the current to swap the poles, then zoom out to the Earth as one large magnet that turns every compass.
takeaway: A magnet's force reaches through space as a field that loops from one pole to the other, and a coil carrying a current is a magnet that can be switched on, off and over.
needsSource: none; the dipole and coil fields are computed, and the strength of Earth's field is a reference value
pitfall: Field lines are a drawing convention, not threads: the field exists everywhere between them. Filings show the field's direction, not its strength; use the compass deflection and the meter for that. Earth's geographic north is a magnetic south pole, which is why a compass's north end points there.
why: AQA GCSE Physics 8463 topic 4.7 'Magnetism and electromagnetism' (permanent and induced magnets, magnetic fields, electromagnets) https://www.aqa.org.uk/subjects/science/gcse/physics-8463/specification-at-a-glance ; AQA KS3 syllabus 3.2.4 'Electromagnets' https://www.oxfordaqa.com/oaqaresources/science/teaching/aqa-science-ks3-syllabus.pdf

The pool's level-0 magnets-and-poles and compass-and-magnetic-poles have no field model and no current.

title: Momentum, impulse & crashes
interaction: Crash two carts head-on with chosen masses, speeds and bounciness, from perfectly elastic to perfectly sticky, and watch the momentum bars before and after. Add a crumple zone or an airbag to one cart and see the force on its passenger drop as the collision is stretched over a longer time, on a force-time graph whose area stays the same. Then fire a cannon on a frozen lake to see the recoil, and play pool on a table where the balls meet at an angle.
takeaway: In every collision the total momentum is unchanged, so what a crumple zone changes is not how much momentum is lost but how long losing it takes, and a longer time means a smaller force.
needsSource: none
pitfall: Momentum is conserved in every collision, including sticky ones; it is kinetic energy that an inelastic collision turns into heat and deformation. A crumple zone does not absorb momentum, it stretches the collision in time.
why: AQA GCSE Physics 8463 topic 4.5.7 'Momentum' (conservation, changes in momentum, safety features) https://filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/physics/specifications/AQA-8463-SP-2016.PDF ; AP Physics 1 Unit 4 'Linear momentum' (impulse, conservation, collisions) https://apstudents.collegeboard.org/courses/ap-physics-1
overlapWith: newtons-laws already collides carts of different mass to show momentum passing between objects; this page keeps that as its first step and adds what it does not show: the bounciness of a collision, impulse as force spread over time (crash safety), recoil and collisions at an angle.

title: Why music has twelve notes
interaction: A keyboard whose keys play, each note drawn as its wave; press two keys and the page plays them together and draws how the waves line up: an octave (double the frequency) every cycle, a fifth (3:2) every two, while clashing pairs beat and a roughness meter rises. Slide a divider to cut the octave into 5, 7, 12, 19 or 31 equal steps and see how close each ladder lands to the simple ratios; twelve lands nearly on the fifth, which is why pianos have twelve keys. Compare an equal-tempered chord with a pure one by ear.
takeaway: Notes sound good together when their frequencies are in simple ratios, and twelve equal steps per octave is the smallest ladder that lands close to those ratios, which is why keyboards have twelve notes.
pitfall: Twelve is a good compromise, not a law of nature or of the ear: other traditions divide the octave differently, and equal temperament makes every fifth slightly flat. Consonance also depends on timbre; the roughness model (Plomp-Levelt 1965) is one measurable part of it.
why: 'Why 12 notes to the octave?' (University of Waterloo) is a widely read answer to a perennial question: https://www.math.uwaterloo.ca/~mrubinst/tuning/12.html
overlapWith: waves-interference: beats and a string's harmonics; this page is which pairs of notes fit together and why the octave is cut into twelve.
needsSource: none (tones synthesized in the browser; the Plomp-Levelt roughness curve is a published formula)

title: Polarized light: sunglasses, screens and the third filter
interaction: Light drawn as a wave wiggling in one direction meets a filter the reader rotates; the fraction that gets through falls from all to none over a quarter turn, plotted against the angle. Cross two filters and nothing passes; slide a third in between at 45° and an eighth of the light comes back, with the wave's direction redrawn after each filter. Then aim the filter at glare off a wet road and rotate it to kill the glare, and look at a phone screen through it.
takeaway: A polarizing filter keeps only the part of a light wave that wiggles along its axis, so two crossed filters block everything, and yet a third filter between them lets light through again.
pitfall: A filter does not let through the photons that were already aligned and block the rest; it projects every wave onto its axis, which is why the middle filter can restore light. Glare is polarized by reflection off horizontal surfaces, not by water being wet.
why: The three-polarizer paradox is a standard demonstration (LibreTexts tutorial), and polarized sunglasses and 3D glasses are everyday objects: https://chem.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Physical_and_Theoretical_Chemistry_Textbook_Maps/Quantum_Tutorials_(Rioux)/07%3A_Quantum_Optics/7.13%3A_The_Three-Polarizer_Paradox
overlapWith: light-optics: bending, focusing and dispersion, with polarization absent. liquid-crystals (pool, level 3) computes the LCD pixel between crossed polarizers; this page stops at the filters and the glare and links there.
needsSource: none

title: Why a spinning ball curves
interaction: Kick, throw or drop a ball with a chosen speed and spin and watch its path bend, with the air drawn flowing past it: the side spinning with the flow carries air round, the air leaves deflected to one side and the ball is pushed to the other. Sliders set spin, speed and the ball (football, tennis, baseball, table tennis, beach ball), and the path curves more for light balls with fast spin; compare a backspin shot that hangs with a topspin shot that dives, and drop a backspinning ball from a dam to watch it sail away from the wall.
takeaway: A spinning ball drags air round with it, so the air leaves it deflected to one side and the ball is pushed to the other: the curve of a free kick, a slice and a topspin lob.
needs: Drag and Magnus-lift coefficients for the balls, from published wind-tunnel measurements, or a documented simplified model stated on the page.
pitfall: Do not explain it with 'faster air on one side, lower pressure' as if the air had to arrive at the same time, the false story the flight page bans; the deflected wake is the honest picture. At low spin a smooth ball can even curve the other way.
why: The backspin basketball dropped from the Gordon Dam (Veritasium with How Ridiculous, 2015) went viral worldwide: https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2015/07/17/423899841/watch-magnus-effect-whisks-basketball-into-the-spin-zone
overlapWith: flight: a wing turns air downward (level 2); this page is the same deflection produced by spin on a ball at level 1, with the ball's whole path shown. newtons-laws has projectiles with drag but no spin.
needsSource: Published coefficient fits (e.g. Goff & Carré 2010 for a football, Nathan 2008 for a baseball), cited; no dataset shipped.

title: Mass, binding energy & the valley of stability
interaction: Scan the chart of all known nuclei, protons against neutrons, coloured by how they decay, with the stable ones running as a valley down the middle; click any nucleus and its measured mass is compared with the mass of its parts, the difference shown as binding energy through E = mc². Follow binding energy per nucleon along the curve from hydrogen to uranium, with the peak near iron, and slide a marker to see why fusing light nuclei and splitting heavy ones both release energy while the middle releases none; pick a decay and watch the daughter land closer to the valley floor.
takeaway: A nucleus weighs less than its parts, the missing mass is the energy holding it together, and because that energy per particle peaks near iron, fusion pays on the light side and fission on the heavy side.
needs: Measured atomic masses and decay modes of all known nuclides.
needsSource: AME2020 and NUBASE2020 from the IAEA Atomic Mass Data Centre: free ASCII files, to be cited through their Chinese Physics C papers (CC BY 3.0); the data files themselves state no licence https://www-nds.iaea.org/amdc
pitfall: Binding energy is not energy stored in the nucleus waiting to come out; it is energy released when the nucleus formed and would have to be put back to take it apart. Iron-56 is not the most tightly bound nucleus, nickel-62 is by a hair; say 'near iron'.
why: AQA A-level Physics 7408 nuclear physics: mass difference and binding energy, binding energy per nucleon, fission and fusion https://senecalearning.com/en-GB/revision-notes/a-level/physics/aqa/8-1-10-binding-energy
overlapWith: nuclear-fission fires neutrons and holds a reactor at criticality, nuclear-fusion heats a plasma, and stars names where elements were made; none shows the curve that explains why either process releases energy, or the chart of nuclides with its valley of stability.

title: The photoelectric effect
interaction: Shine light on a metal plate in a vacuum tube and watch electrons leave, or not: slide the colour from red toward ultraviolet and nothing happens until a threshold, then electrons appear at once however dim the light; turn up the intensity and more electrons leave but none faster. Apply a reverse voltage to stop them and plot the stopping voltage against frequency: a straight line whose slope is Planck's constant and whose intercept is the metal's work function; change the metal and the line shifts but keeps its slope. A side panel shows what a wave model predicts and where it fails.
takeaway: Light delivers its energy in packets whose size depends only on colour, so dim blue light frees electrons that bright red light never can, and the graph's slope is the same for every metal.
needs: Work functions of a few metals (sodium, potassium, zinc, copper, platinum).
needsSource: reference constants (CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics; the values are facts reproduced in textbooks); no dataset
pitfall: Brighter light does not give faster electrons, and there is no delay while a dim beam charges up the metal; both are the wave model's failed predictions and should be shown failing, not merely stated.
why: AQA A-level Physics 7408 topic 3.2.2.1 'The photoelectric effect' (threshold frequency, work function, stopping potential) https://www.tutopiya.com/tools/uk-revision-checklist/aqa-alevel/physics ; PhET's 'Photoelectric Effect' is a widely used classroom simulation https://script.spoken-tutorial.org/index.php/PhET/C2/Photoelectric-Effect/English
overlapWith: quantum-mechanics (level 3) starts at the double slit and tunnelling, and solar-cells (level 2) uses photons freeing electrons in a junction; the experiment that first showed light comes in packets, and the graph that measures Planck's constant, is on neither.

title: Entanglement & Bell's theorem
interaction: Send pairs of entangled particles to two stations and set each station's measurement angle. First program the particles with any hidden instruction table you like and run thousands of pairs: the CHSH correlation never passes 2. Then switch the source to quantum mechanics and the simulated stations climb to 2.83; overlay the counts from the 2015 Delft experiment, which reached 2.42 with its error bar clear of 2.
takeaway: No set of pre-agreed answers can push the correlation past 2, quantum mechanics predicts up to 2.83, and the real experiment measured 2.42, above the classical bound.
needs: Delft loophole-free Bell test data (Hensen et al. 2015), 4TU.ResearchData doi:10.4121/uuid:6e19e9b2-4a2d-40b5-8dd3-a660bf3c0a31, under the 4TU General Terms of Use (open access but not a CC licence; the page works without it).
pitfall: Entanglement sends no message: each station's own results are coin flips whatever the other does, and only the comparison afterwards shows the correlation.
why: Veritasium's Bell-test explainer, among the most watched quantum videos: https://www.sciencealert.com/watch-this-is-how-quantum-entanglement-really-works
overlapWith: quantum-computing: entangles two qubits and compares results; this page pits those results against every possible hidden-variable strategy and shows the inequality broken.
needsSource: 4TU.ResearchData, 4TU General Terms of Use (open, not CC); weak as a shipped dataset, optional.

title: Bifurcations & nonlinear dynamics
interaction: Slide one parameter of a flow on the line or the plane and watch its fixed points move, collide and vanish (saddle-node), split in two (pitchfork) or give birth to a limit cycle (Hopf), with the bifurcation diagram drawn as you go and the vector field animated beside it. Then apply the same slider to real systems: a laser crossing threshold, a beam that buckles, a neuron that starts firing.
takeaway: A smooth change in a parameter can produce a sudden change in behaviour, and a handful of bifurcation types account for nearly all of them.
pitfall: Chaos is not the subject: the logistic map and the double pendulum stay on chaos-fractals, and this page concerns what happens to equilibria of continuous flows before any chaos appears.
why: MIT OCW 8.09 Classical Mechanics III, chapter 7 on chaos and nonlinear dynamics with Strogatz as the text: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/pages/syllabus
overlapWith: chaos-fractals: covers the logistic map's period doubling and chaos; this page covers the saddle-node, pitchfork and Hopf bifurcations of continuous flows that come before chaos.
needsSource: none

title: Blackbody radiation from counting modes
interaction: Set the size and temperature of a cavity; the page counts the standing-wave modes in each frequency band and assigns each its average energy. Give every mode kT and the total runs off to infinity at high frequency; give each Planck's quantized average and the familiar hump appears. Overlay the COBE FIRAS spectrum of the cosmic microwave background and slide the temperature until it fits.
takeaway: The blackbody spectrum is the number of wave modes times the average energy of each, and only a quantized average keeps the high-frequency end from exploding.
needs: COBE FIRAS CMB monopole spectrum (Fixsen et al. 1996), firas_monopole_spec_v1.txt from NASA LAMBDA; NASA data, public domain.
pitfall: Planck quantized the oscillators of the cavity wall, not light itself; the page must not present the derivation as the discovery of the photon.
why: PhET lists 'Blackbody Spectrum' (HTML5) among its quantum simulations: https://phet.colorado.edu/en/search?q=Planck
overlapWith: stars: uses the blackbody curve to colour stars by temperature; this page derives the curve by counting modes and shows exactly where classical physics fails.
needsSource: NASA LAMBDA, https://lambda.gsfc.nasa.gov/product/cobe/firas_monopole_spect.html; US government data, public domain.

title: Quantum statistics & Bose-Einstein condensation
interaction: Fill the ladder of levels of a trap with identical particles and cool them: with Boltzmann statistics the occupation thins out smoothly, with bosons a macroscopic fraction drops into the ground level below a critical temperature, with fermions the levels stack up to a Fermi energy. A plot tracks the condensate fraction against temperature, and beside it the 1995 JILA velocity distributions of rubidium show the same peak appearing.
takeaway: Whether particles may share a state decides a gas's whole thermal behaviour: bosons pile into one state when cold, fermions never can.
needs: JILA/NIST 1995 rubidium velocity-distribution images (credit NIST/JILA/CU-Boulder); NIST material, public domain in the US.
pitfall: Condensation needs no attraction at all: it happens in an ideal gas purely because the particles are indistinguishable, so the page must not explain it as the atoms sticking together.
why: MIT OCW 8.044 syllabus notes Bose gases and Bose-Einstein condensation as the one modern addition to the course: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-044-statistical-physics-i-spring-2013/pages/syllabus
overlapWith: states-of-matter: condenses a gas through attraction; here a gas condenses with no forces at all, purely because its particles are indistinguishable.
needsSource: NIST image gallery, 'Bose-Einstein condensate' 1995 (NIST/JILA/CU-Boulder); public domain as NIST work, to be confirmed on NIST's own page.

title: Brownian motion & the Einstein relation
interaction: Step through Einstein's and Perrin's argument with a live model at each stage: a grain in a bath of molecules is kicked at random (a Langevin simulation), its mean squared displacement grows in proportion to time, the slope depends on temperature, viscosity and grain size, and Perrin's 1909 displacement counts fall on the predicted Gaussian. The last step turns the slope into Avogadro's number.
takeaway: A visible grain's random jitter grows with the square root of time, and the rate of that growth counts the molecules in a mole.
needs: Perrin's displacement counts for gamboge grains (Annales de Chimie et de Physique, 1909); public domain.
pitfall: Displacement grows with the square root of time, not time; a Brownian grain has no measurable velocity, which is why Perrin measured displacements.
why: Princeton COS 126 'Atomic Nature of Matter' assignment, which has students repeat Perrin's estimate of Avogadro's number from Brownian displacements: https://introcs.cs.princeton.edu/java/assignments/atomic.html
overlapWith: central-limit-theorem: sums random variables in the abstract; this page is the physical random walk and the measurement that turned it into a count of molecules.
needsSource: Perrin, 'Mouvement brownien et réalité moléculaire', Ann. Chim. Phys. 1909; public domain (author died 1942).

title: The Casimir effect
interaction: Slide two mirrors toward each other inside a one-dimensional cavity; the page lists the standing-wave modes that still fit between them and outside, adds up their zero-point energies with an adjustable high-frequency cutoff, and shows the difference settling to a finite value that does not depend on the cutoff. The resulting force is plotted against separation.
takeaway: Constraining which waves can exist between two plates lowers the vacuum energy between them, and the plates feel that as an attraction that grows steeply as they approach.
pitfall: The force is not evidence of a vast tappable energy in the vacuum, and it can equally be computed from fluctuating charges in the plates; say so.
why: Wikipedia 'Casimir effect', a perennial 'how does it work' question whose popular explanation is disputed on the page itself: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casimir_effect
overlapWith: blackbody-cavity-modes: counts the same cavity modes with thermal energy; here it is their zero-point energy and the force it exerts.
needsSource: none
